newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Environment Council to hold Sunday session on climate.
newsitem.headline: Environment Council to hold Sunday session on climate.

text.p: Environment ministers will gather in Brussels on Sunday evening to try to fix an EU position on cutting greenhouse gas emissions, a vain goal for now according to Dutch EU minister Margreet de Boer.

De Boer, who called the unusual early start to the regular environment council scheduled for Monday and Tuesday, told a news conference earlier this week that a deal was unlikely ahead of the June Council.

The session will nevertheless give ministers their first opportunity to comment on the presidency's push to put some beef into what has been a long and inconclusive debate on what the EU should do on climate change.

The Sunday timing is an attempt by the Dutch to firm EU thinking ahead of the March 3-7 meeting in Bonn of the ad hoc group on the Berlin climate change convention mandate, which is set to continue work towards a global accord.
Next on ministers' agenda will be a draft resolution on the Commission's communication about improving implementation of environment law.

EU officials said the March Council was intended to reach agreement in principle on the text ahead of its probable adoption in June, after the European Parliament has completed its own resolution on the communication.
The next point, to be discussed by ministers over lunch on Monday in the absence of their aides, will cover the latest developments in the leg-hold trap debate and Regulation 3254/91.

Traps were the subject of much sound and fury in December when ministers called for tougher trap norms to be negotiated between the EU, Canada, Russia and the United States while at the same time ordering the Commission to prepare fall-back legal texts for a fur import ban to begin at the end of March.

Monday's talks are likely to be less heated given the instructions issued by this week's General Affairs Council, which were for the Commission to get on with talks with a view to reporting back preferably before the end of March and in any case before June's Environment Council.
Discussions will then move to the Commission's Auto/Oil proposals, COM(96)248, which ministers first discussed in an open session on October 15 in Luxembourg.

EU officials said the main points at issue would be the limit emission values and fuel quality standards for the year 2000, and, the question of whether or not to make indicative 2005 targets compulsory now or whether to wait for the end of 1998 as proposed by the Commission.
No decision is expected before June, by which time the European Parliament is likely to have completed its first reading on the different texts.
Officials predicted political agreement for a common position on the decision for a Community action programme promoting environmental non-governmental organisations.

The proposal for NGO co-financing, intended to run from January 1998 to the end of 2001, would earmark 10.6 million Ecus to be used in funding up to half of a qualifying organisation's budgeted activity.

Ministers will then move on to a discussion of the Commission's communication on environmental agreements, with the Dutch asking for remarks to be geared towards whether such instruments could be effective at EU level and whether they could replace environmental legislation.

Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard will then present the Commission's proposal for a directive intended to limit emissions of volatile organic compounds from certain processes and industrial installations, COM(96)538.

Ministers are then scheduled to meet their counterparts from the central and eastern European countries (CEECs), namely Estonia, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia.
The Commission will present a report on the state of work to approximate the different countries' environmental legislation with that of the EU.
Ministers will then debate "climate change and environmental policy: a challenge for energy conservation".

Five questions on the table cover the likely long-term effects of climate change, how EU countries and CEECs might develop a joint approach in global climate change negotiations, joint implementation possibilties between EU and CEECs and whether further work on energy conservation projects is need.
The final agenda item, which does not include the CEECs, concerns the Commission's recently adopted proposal for a framework directive on water policy.
